context_blurb:
Living things make offspring in two ways. In asexual reproduction, one parent makes clones, offspring with exactly its genes. In sexual reproduction, cells from two parents join, and each offspring gets a new mix of genes. A bread bag, a pond and a garden show both at work.

Before a bacterium divides, it copies the loop that holds nearly all its genes, then splits in two, so both new cells have the same genes as the first cell, barring rare copying mistakes. At one split every 20 minutes, a single cell can become over a million in under seven hours.

Baker's yeast, a one-celled fungus, uses both ways. While food lasts, each cell buds off a little copy of itself. When food runs out, yeast can turn to sexual reproduction and form spores, shuffling its genes. Its offspring then vary, so if conditions change, some may cope better than the parent would; a new mix is not better by rule, only different. The spores are also tough resting cells, with thick walls that stand up to heat until food returns.

Moulds spread mostly by spores too small to see, which float in the air indoors and out. Mould turns up on a sealed loaf because spores drifting in the air settled on it as it cooled or was sliced, and each grew into a new mould, a copy of its parent. In the 1700s the Italian botanist Pier Antonio Micheli tested spontaneous generation, the mistaken old idea that fungi spring from food itself, by setting spores on melon slices: up came the very kind of fungus that had shed them.

A planarian, a small pond flatworm, is full of stem cells, which can build any missing part. Cut one in half across the middle, and the front half regrows a tail while the back half regrows a head, so each piece grows into a whole worm within a few weeks. Some planarians pinch in two on their own.

A strawberry spreads by runners, long creeping stems that root a little plant at each end. Grown from the parent's own stem, every runner plant is a clone with exactly its genes, which is how growers spread a good strawberry. Each seed on the berry, though, formed when a cell from a pollen grain joined an egg cell in the flower, so every seedling has a new mix of genes.

Cycads, cone-bearing plants, grow as separate males and females, and a seed forms only when a male's pollen reaches an ovule, a seed-to-be, on a female's cones. In 1895 the botanist John Medley Wood found one wild cycad at a forest's edge in South Africa, and no other has turned up. Gardeners have grown hundreds more from shoots at its base, but Wood's plant was a male and shoots are clones, so all are males, cloned from one male plant, and none can set seed.

In a flower, the stamens make pollen and the pistil holds the ovules in its ovary. Pollination, the carrying of pollen to the pistil, is often done by animals paid in sugary nectar. Bees see ultraviolet light, which people cannot. Photographed in ultraviolet, a meadow buttercup's yellow petals show dark near the flower's centre, where the nectar lies: a nectar guide, which steers a bee quickly to its reward. Bees cannot see red, though. Red, scentless tubes brimming with watery nectar suit a hummingbird, since birds find flowers by sight and have a poor sense of smell. Moth and bat flowers are mostly pale or dull and strongly scented, though such patterns are tendencies, not rules.

Wind carries corn's pollen from the tassel on top to the silks below, each the long tip of one tiny flower, joined to one future kernel. A kernel forms only where a pollen grain lands on its silk, sticks fast and sends a tube down to the ovule. In a single row, much of the pollen blows away from the ears, so too little reaches many silks and the ears come out gappy; garden guides advise a block of at least three or four short rows.

Once a cell from the pollen has fertilized, or joined, the egg cell in each ovule, the ovules ripen into seeds and the ovary swells into the fruit around them. So a pea pod, grown from the flower's ovary, is a fruit, and each pea is a seed; tomatoes and cucumbers are fruits too, sweet or not.
